I've had pretty much no life the last few days, so as someone with all bosses + most achievements done, here are my thoughts (no spoilers):

I personally feel that the online journalism doom and gloom is overblown. This game is sick, and it's some of the most fun I've had playing a game in a while. I am fairly confident that future updates (duos, more content, possibly hard mode) will only reinforce this sentiment. I think it's an 8-9/10 and easily worth the purchase. With that said, here are my pros/cons:

Pros:
[list]
[*]Combat is excellent. Movesets and fighting styles from various games (poise tanking from DS1, Sekiro perfect parry, Bloodborne mobility, etc.) are all available and feel great. The skills/arts are a super interesting addition. 
[*]The bosses are very fun and beautifully designed. If you're not targeting their elemental weakness (shown before you queue up on an expedition), prepare for it to feel unfair. This mistake is where a lot of "this game is BS" complaints come from.
[*]One of my biggest Elden Ring complaints was that the "open world" format felt empty when 90%+ of consumables/item drops weren't things I would/could use given my build. This is addressed in this game. Holding weapons in your inventory will give you their passive statuses, and almost every consumable is good. I stumble on a variety of decent loot every minute.
[*]The gameplay loop both in/out of expeditions are great. Each character has "remembrances" (questlines) that you can complete. Completing them gives you rewards. This, along with relic customization, gives you meaningful things to work toward even when you don't succeed in a given expedition. Inside expeditions, it's fast-paced (you're making constant decisions based on RNG) and has plenty of high risk/high reward paths that make it exciting. 
[*]Build variety is insane. I've gone bow Raider, colossal Duchess, madness caster, and more (and made it work) using various special relics and run-based drops. Even how you play - which ruins/camps/field bosses you run to in which order - can be dictated by their locations and how you kitted your relics before the game. As you progress, your options will expand.
[*]The OST and visuals are gorgeous. 
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
[*]The game seems to have issues with newer graphics cards. Some of my friends have been crashing constantly. You can rejoin, but you lose a level and need to pick up your runes as if you had died. These hardware compatibility issues need some patching. 
[*]The choice of passive status effects you get after defeating great enemies would benefit from more variety. Some of the options (I'm talking about you, "flask slowly restores hp") are almost strictly bad, and I think there tend to be too few options in general. I think expanding on this would really polish the game's roguelike elements.
[*]The game could use some scalable content. In previous titles, that was NG+. An endless night/hard mode/etc. is something I would like to see. As of right now, you cannot scale the difficulty unless you handicap yourself.
[*]While there is procedural generation that keeps gameplay relatively fresh, there is only one main map. I would love to see new terrains/maps just to mix things up.
[/list]

There are plenty of things to discuss regarding this game, but I think these hit the main points (in my opinion). Overall, the game is a blast, and I foresee it improving in future updates. I definitely recommend it.

Review from the perspective of a dad with very limited time:

Honestly, a terrible choice if you’re looking for a quick gaming session.
A single run can take up to 40 minutes, and since you cannot pause the game, this becomes a real problem — especially in Duo or Trio.

You cannot simply pause an online multiplayer game!
So be warned: you need a proper time slot to play this game in peace. This is not a “jump in for 10 minutes” kind of experience.

That said:
It takes a while to get used to the pace — but once it clicks… oh boy, this game absolutely slaps.
The power spikes hit hard, and when everything comes together, it feels insanely good.

Despite the time commitment issues:
9/10 Soulslike — amazing gameplay, just not parent-friendly.

Amazing game concept, just feels like its missing about half of content. More bosses, more randomized, more enemy types and weapons to start. New playable characters and some minor bug fixes and you have a great game.

This is the closest we'll ever get to an Elden Ring-style co-op PvE experience, and it's amazing.

Let’s get the most important thing out of the way first:
✅ No battle pass
✅ No microtransactions
✅ No Paid BS

Everything is included, and some content is even hidden in a way that many players won’t ever find. I guarantee a ton of people haven’t even unlocked the Revenant class yet. If this were EA, Ubisoft, or Activision, they’d be selling that class for $40.

People complaining about the lack of duo mode? It’s already solved with a mod. And FromSoft isn’t trying to block it. They even let you disable Easy Anti-Cheat and mod the game freely, or just play offline solo. What other multiplayer game lets you do that these days?

This is a rare chance to support a game that isn’t built around greed or FOMO. That alone is worth something.

Now for the real talk:
If you have two friends, this game is a blast. Communicate on Discord, plan your route, take on the night together, it feels like a full campaign co-op experience.
If you have one friend, grab the duo mod and you're still set.
(thanks weszty for reminding me, fromsoft is also planing to add dou to the game)
If you're solo... That’s where things get rough.

Yes, there are good runs with randoms who "get it," and those moments shine. But most of the time, it’s chaos. One guy is running off to fight a level 10 boss solo for no reason while the rest of the team is halfway across the map. You’ll spend more time confused than progressing.

There's no in-game voice chat (Souls tradition), just emotes(gestures), talk items, and pin drops. It works in its own cryptic way, but for random matchmaking, it’s far from ideal.
Luckily, I play with friends now, so this isn't a problem for me anymore. But if you’re going in alone, you really need to love Souls-style gameplay to stick with it.

Gameplay?
Smooth as butter. You’re not supposed to clear the whole map. You choose what to tackle, who to fight, where to go. Make strategic decisions, scale your power, survive the night, and fight the Nightlord.
Some say the night cycle is too fast, but no, it’s perfect. This isn’t a slow, scenic open-world. You need to move, adapt, and level up quickly.

Bosses hard? Of course. It's a Souls-like. They’re supposed to be hard. You’ll get smacked, but it’s fair. There’s a revive system, and if you play smart, aggro, revive, coordinate, you’ll get your fair shot at each fight.

Some folks hate the revive system. They’re wrong. It’s genius. Your attack opportunities are a resource, and spending them to bring a teammate back creates high-stakes moments that feel earned.

First revive: 3-4 hits

Second: 6-7 hits

Third? Let’s just say… good luck.
But characters like Guardian, Executor, Recluse, and especially Revenant can turn the tide and revive the whole squad like heroes.

In conclusion:
If you’ve got a friend or two, get it. You’ll have a hell of a time.
If you’re solo… tread carefully unless you’re a hardcore Souls fan.

While this game does suffer from a lot of missed potential, ELDEN RING NIGHTREIGN and its DLC provide hundreds of hours of fun; it easily kept my friends and I hooked and grinding for months. The main idea of NIGHTREIGN is to condense the classic ELDEN RING experience down into a 45 minute run with randomized bosses, points of interest and weapons, and make it cooperatively playable up to 3 people.

ELDEN RING NIGHTEIGN isn't exactly a roguelike, but it definitely plays like one. And a kind of weak one, at that. It's not a big deal at all when you first start playing, but becomes more apparent as you rack up hours. This game's biggest flaw is its lack of randomization in its experiences, leading to fatigue and runs ultimately not feeling significantly different from each other. This problem is helped by the addition of the  DLC's content, but there are still many "What If?" moments. What if they could have added Shadow of the Erdtree weapons? What if there were twice as many legacy Dark Souls bosses? What if the POI's weren't so formulaic? If you are a massive roguelike fan, you may find other games in the genre to far surpass NIGHTREIGN's random elements. 

Basically everything else is so great though. The FROMSOFT combat and gameplay formula is more fun than ever, with new additions to the sandbox unique to NIGHTREIGN. The super sprint added brings the pace up to a blistering level and it's addicting to dart around the map.  All playable characters are so much fun to play and master, with different costumes to acquire and relics to customize your loadout. All the bosses pose a feasible challenge and remain a blast to learn. 

NIGHTREIGN's best aspect are the ten final NIGHTBOSSES. They are completely original bosses with insane spectacle, challenge, and sense of reward for overcoming. Taking on each one and finally managing to conquer them alongside two friends still hasn't lost its luster. These are some of the greatest bosses FROMSOFT have ever created. Most of them have an alternate 'hard mode' version, with difficulty cranked to 11 and insane alternate movesets. 

Post launch, FROMSOFT added a "ranked mode" called Deep of Night, and it provides a massive challenge as well. This hard mode, alongside the added "hard mode" bosses offer tons of replayability. This game is an absolute blast, and will remain in rotation with my friends for a while. 

If you can't get enough FROMSOFT and you have a few friends willing to take the plunge, this is an easy recommend.

“Brutal. Beautiful. Best with friends.”
Nightreign isn’t here to welcome you — it’s here to break you. Time-limited runs, shrinking maps, and zero handholding. You either work as a team, or you die fast and confused.

The co-op design is incredible. Each class plays differently and actually matters. Bosses? Top-tier FromSoft chaos. Every fight feels like an event. The roguelike loop keeps things fresh and addictively tense.

Matchmaking feels barebones, and the fact that there’s still no crossplay — in a co-op game, in 2025 — honestly makes no sense. Some zones and enemies look like they were lifted straight out of Elden Ring, which kind of takes the edge off what should’ve felt like a completely new world. And while the mood and setting are solid, the storytelling isn’t really the focus here — don’t go in expecting deep lore or that classic FromSoftware mystery. It’s all about the moment-to-moment tension.

TL;DR:
Nightreign can be rough, especially if you’re playing solo. The matchmaking sucks, there’s no crossplay, and yeah — some areas feel like Elden Ring leftovers. But get two solid friends on voice chat, and suddenly it all clicks. The tension, the coordination, the chaos — it’s intense in the best way. It’s not perfect, but when it works, it really works.

To set expectations straight, this game isn’t a soulsborne with training wheels, it’s a storm you’re meant to weather. An unapologetically challenging experience crafted to test your resilience, adaptability, and patience. It forges crucibles from discomfort, silence, and failure. You’re meant to lose, adapt, and grow, that’s the core philosophy of the game.

The format revolves around tense expeditions and bursts of pressure. You speedrun through series of boss fights, pushing to survive the night, gear up, level up, and face the final boss. Win or lose, you return with runes and relics that shape your next attempt. It’s a compact system that both respects your time and demands full attention, every failure build your progression and every victory feels earned. 

Each expedition is a loop: go in, get crushed, come back smarter. The true power lies in mastering your map, your gear, and your chalice. You learn which relics make or break a run. Some are situational, others indispensable, and some will seem worthless until you figure out where they shine. The relic system, armaments, and buffs don’t just hand you a build; they help you craft the best version of your class. Critics who dismiss it as 'just 8 bosses and a reskin' miss what lies beneath the surface. Progression doesn’t lie in a linear gear treadmill, it lies in how well you adapt your playstyle, and exploit your gear and upgrades. The buildcrafting here isn’t loud or flashy it’s patient and subtle. Long runbacks test your patience more than reflexes, but that’s part of what makes FromSoftware titles feel earned. They don’t aim to please everyone with only one active objective per player. This isn’t a flaw, but an inherent part of the game’s structure. It’s an adjustment players need to make embracing the repeated challenges to progress, rather than expecting a constant flow of new objectives.

The multiplayer system is straightforward, with a simple quest structure. Trio mode feels balanced, though bosses health bars are deliberately inflated. With three nightfarers raids become manageable as long as you coordinate. You can still play with a friend and have a third player join in without a password, but if they quit, your duo will struggle, as the difficulty doesn’t scale down. Solo play adapts to your skill level, but sometimes, you'll face triple-boss spawns or raids, just like in trio mode and that can feel overwhelming. The revive mechanic shifts the pacing; you’re not undead or unkindled anymore, but a reliable companion where teamwork is a skill to master, especially in this game.

The frustration about voice chat misses a key point: FromSoft’s summon system has always centered on limited communication by design. We survived with trolling messages, bloodstains, audible carvings/prattling pates, and gestures while co-oping with a summon. There is communication, it just isn’t what mainstream games train you to expect. Letting gameplay speak for itself is a feature, not a flaw. It builds a stronger sense of self-reliance and discovery. The summoning systems have always meant more, they’ve been a way to forge real connections. Through simple gestures and item sharing, I’ve experienced a coop that feels far more genuine than voice chat ever could.

On the technical side, there are a few limitations like 60fps caps, frame drops, and no support for ultrawide resolutions or crossplay. HDR appears flat in its current state. These factors don’t impact core gameplay but are important considerations for those looking for a fully optimized experience. Crossplay, in particular, would simplify matchmaking and help maintain a healthy player base.

This game isn’t trying to hold your hand or your wallet. It offers a brutal yet elegant challenge and says: “figure it out.” It’s lean, maybe even raw, but purposeful. It doesn’t promise endless content updates or seasonal filler and I'm okay with that. Not every game needs to grow endlessly to justify itself.

[h1]Good Spinoff, Bad Roguelite[/h1]

I always have a mixed feeling towards Elden Ring Nightreign. The extraction-style gameplay shuns me away for quite a while. But after playing it through, I certainly feel less dismissive about it. On one hand, it's admirable to see FromSoft step out of their comfort zone and try something different. Yet on the other hand, Nightreign is not a particularly good roguelite experience. Even some of the indie brethren can eclipse its effort. Still, Nightreign is an interesting experiment on mixing up different mechanics from popular genres. It's better to bring a friend or two along. Solo is certainly doable, but the learning curve is steep.

[h2]Thing I Like About Elden Ring Nightreign:[/h2]

[list]
[*][b]The Raids:[/b] Now I think about it. The Radahn fight in the base game is definitely the prototype behind Nightreign. You and your friends working together to take on (or cheese the hell out of) a big boss is one of the best moments in the Souls series. Nightreign tries to expertize this experience, and I say it's a job well-done. Scout the map, plan the route, conquer locations, loot the gear, run away from the shrinking zone, defeat two ring bosses, tackle the Nightlord and fail miserably (prerequisite). A complex process on the surface, but with friends you can easily make it fun. Moreover, teamwork has never been more important than ever. Who draws aggro, who deals damage, and when to rotate the roles for breathing room, [strike] and stop going after the Bell-bearing A-hole[/strike] are key to a successful expedition.

[*][b]Preset Characters:[/b] I am a little bit sad you can't create your own character, but at least the eight available ones are very unique. Each of them offers a distinctive playstyle and fulfills a certain role in your team. You can find your preferred playstyle in these characters. Moreover, their backstories are also interesting, told through FromSoft's usual storytelling shenanigans, except this time it's rather clear and more involved in the player's part. I like how these people feel like a bunch of misfits bound together by a shared goal. Yet, through remembrance you can easily see how their fate intertwined with each other. 

[*][b]Combat QOL Improvements:[/b] Now these are something that sparks excitement not only for the game but also for future titles. Nightreign has a lot of improvements on both combat and movement. Instant sprint offers a new way to close gaps and make distance. Jump has been even better at dodging attacks since the inclusion of kick/wall jump. Enemies' grab attacks are now unifyingly color-coded for easier recognition. There's also a red marker on the character indicating who is being targeted by the boss right now. Performing a critical attack no longer makes the enemies invulnerable, meaning your teammates can continuously wail on their downfalls. Whips, shields, and even bows can now backstab, and so on.
[/list]

[h2]Things I Like And Dislike About Elden Ring Nightreign:[/h2]

[list]
[*][b]Shifting Earth:[/b] Nightreign's map is pretty stale. The random generation doesn't alter the map layout much, so the developers create this feature to mitigate the problem. Unfortunately, Shifting Earth only achieved half of its goal. For the good parts, these new biomes drastically change parts of Limveld. They offer new terrains, special points of interest and a unique secret buff for you to uncover. However, the way the developers implement leaves a lot to be desired. They are randomized one "period" at a time. The game rolls one event, and the next few runs you will always have this event active (unless you sleep). These new terrains also suffer from the same issue as the mainland—fixed placement and fixed layout. I really wish their locations could be randomized, and the other terrains could have the chance to spawn as sub-areas. 

[*][b]Nightlords:[/b] Just like the eight playable characters, all eight Nightlords are fantastic in their own way. The classic orchestral bombardment is in full force. Their presentations are easily the most stunning out of all the Souls series. Their move sets are designed to deal with multiple targets at once, and there are actual interesting mechanics woven in to make the fights more dynamic. The only thing I really dislike about the boss design is the cinematic attack—you know, the one where you see the boss fly away and you wait for almost 10 seconds until it lands that one attack. This is a trend I wish Fromsoft would refrain from using too much. It only works once. The second and third times onward just feel like a waste of time. Oh, and also fck Maris.
[/list]

[h2]Things I Dislike About Elden Ring Nightreign:[/h2]

[list]
[*][b]Relics:[/b] It's farming blood gems in Chalice Dungeons all over again...except it's worst and takes longer to get. I believe the purpose of the relics is to make your early game as smooth as possible. If that's the case, then there are two problems. First of all, the pool is heavily diluted by tons of weak or borderline useless attributes. Even if you manage to roll a stat-boosting one, the number is still too negligible to make a difference. Second, everything is completely randomized. There is no way to reroll attributes, so the only way to get better relics is gambling. 

[*][b]Builds:[/b] This might be me not adjusting my mindset accordingly, so take it with a grain of salt. Despite introducing character abilities and passive bonuses, the build flexibility is surprisingly rigid in Nightreign. One of the beautiful things in Souls games is how easily and freely you can change your build. Nightreign doesn't do that. All characters have set stats, and leveling up gives a universal increase to every stat. As a result, it's easier to lean into what the character is already capable of instead of exploring other possibilities. Passives on weapons might enable a certain degree of availability, but it will never be half as good as a dedicated build. 
[/list]

[b]中文小簡評[/b]
一開始《艾爾登法環黑夜君臨》讓我五味雜陳，強調快速清塔撿裝躲圈的設計與FromSoft一貫照自己步調細細探索的作風大相逕庭，讓我望之卻步，直到夏特才決定入手來體驗，把玩幾場後我算是體悟出箇中滋味。《黑夜君臨》是FromSoft踏出舒適圈的一次大膽嘗試，將既有的魂系戰鬥與現今較熱門遊戲類別的機制加以融合，的確打造出獨具風味的遊戲體驗，這份勇氣值得嘉許。然而以roguelite的角度去看的話機制非常不成熟，幾乎被其他獨立同儕輾壓。不過最好還是拉個朋友一起入坑，單人打可行，就是學習曲線過於坎坷。

[b]喜歡的點[/b]
[list]
    [*]現在想來，《艾爾登法環》裡的碎星Boss戰應該就是《黑夜君臨》的藍圖吧！和朋友一起挑戰（或用各種外鄉手段）打Boss絕對是魂系遊戲中最最棒的體驗之一。《黑夜君臨》在這點上就發揮的淋漓盡致，一起觀察地形、一起規劃路線、一起分工、一起跑圈撿裝、一起打黑夜王然後再一起被壓在地上磨擦。
    [*]這也是歷代魂系中最講究團隊合作的重要性，誰負責坦傷、誰負責輸出、何時要輪替吸仇恨製造喘息空間、誰要去阻止隊友在等級太低的情況下還敢去打鈴珠獵人和龍形大樹守衛，這些流程看似複雜，但和朋友一同經歷就能充分享受其中樂趣。
    [*]不能自創角色有點可惜，但遊戲提供的八位主角各具特色，各自擁有鮮明的定位與專精的武器，絕對能讓你找到自己心儀的玩法。此外，他們的背景故事也很有趣，除了FromSoftware一往的敘事手法外，也加入了許多互動要素，讓你能更清楚了解他們。我意外地滿喜歡這群看似格格不入的烏合之眾，只是因為共同的目標而聚集在一起。然而，透過追憶你就能明白他們彼此的命運緊密交織在一起。
    [*]不過我最喜歡的還是本作在戰鬥方面做的各種改良，像是瞬間衝刺讓你能快速逃離或拉近與Boss間的距離、、敵人抓技有用更鮮明的特效顯示、Boss打出大招時也能清楚看出誰被鎖定、爆擊或背刺敵人時隊友可以無視無敵禎盡情輸出等，這些都是很棒的設計，讓人非常期待FromSoft未來遊戲的走向。
[/list]

[b]又愛又恨的點[/b]
[list]
    [*]《黑夜君臨》的地圖變化隨機性低且非常單調，通常走過一次就能輕鬆記起來，因此製作團隊想用「特異地形」來做點變化，我只能說這項設計只做到一半。先說優點，特異地形的確有效改變部分主地圖的地形，加入了新敵人、新地點以及專屬隱藏增益讓你能在規劃路線上做些改變。但是呢，特異地形是以隨機「週期性」的方式出現， 一旦條件生成你接下來的所有行動都會是出同一個地形，而且這些特異地形也跟主地圖有同樣的問題：位置與分部始終固定，沒有隨機地點，也沒有隨機生成特殊子區域實屬可惜。
    [*]黑夜王的表現各有千秋，氣勢與演出絕對不輸FromSoft過去的經典Boss，配樂一個比一個還有特色，招式上不僅充分考量「一對多」的要素，也成功融入有趣且非一面倒的機制，這在正統魂系中可是非常少見的。缺點的話，我覺得FromSoft可以少用點浮誇的攻擊，這裡是指那種Boss會突然走遠遠的開始搞一些很炫泡的前置，然後過來打你一下。第一次感覺很新鮮很壯麗，但兩、三次後難免會覺得有點浪費時間。
[/list]

[b]不喜歡的點[/b]
[list]
    [*]遺物機制根本就是下位版的金盃刷血寶石啊！即使退一萬步說遺物的功能只是用來讓你前期好過一些好了，詞條全靠隨機生成，既沒有鎖詞條重刷其他欄位的功能，還將一些改變角色技藝或絕活的重要詞條與一堆非常無用的詞條放在一起，讓人刷起來非常氣餒。
    [*]這點應該歸究於我個人心境還沒調適過來。《黑夜君臨》看似有許多被動與技能可搭配，實際上角色流派的多樣性與變化性比想像中來的侷限。本作不像《艾爾登法環》可以隨時隨地改變配點裝備，角色初始數值固定，升等也自動幫你配好點，與其探索其他可能性倒不如更專心玩角色已經擅長的流派。
[/list]

(This wasn't me getting carried btw, I typically play the tank so I'm the one taking majority of the aggro and dodging, its just that the game just got so much more efficient when you can actually talk to each other.)

The game at core is good, but for your own sake play with voice chat, otherwise you are in for a miserable time. You don't need actual friends (although that does elevate any experience), but you do DEFINITELY need a way to comm strategy, items and pathing. The vast majority of people understand how this game works believe me, its very easy to find a decent team.

I'm cutting it some slack in the balance and bug department since this is a new venture for Fromsoft, and its only been out for a few days, but there are definitely issues that are hard to ignore:

- Aformentioned lack of even a basic ping wheel, much less voice chat, in a game this diverse and strategic.

- Matchmaking pool is splintered into so many unnecessary subsections that cant match with each other that it really is going to kill the game once the initial spike in players drops and stabilizes.

- Lotta bugs, multiplayer-related and otherwise (e.g I finished a tough sidequest where you had to kill a boss with a specific character but it didn't register??? So there goes a lot of effort for no reason).

- Lots of bosses have Consort Radahn levels of frame-killer moves that can freeze or even crash a pc regardless of specs.

-  What is especially boring this game down for me is I found that there is a surprising lack of actual effective variety to experience once you play this game enough. There's plenty of loot and gacha relics with random effects for builds, but at the end of the day its very limited which ones are actually viable/useful.



Despite all these problems, At the end of the day I actually have fun with the expeditions with vc and especially progressing the characters' stories/remembrances. While I do think though this game could be a smidge cheaper considering how many assets are reused and reliance on multiplayer, and being able to trade or at least borrow relics from each other should be implemented pronto, this game is still worth it if you can cough up the moolah.

From the very start, I thought this concept was interesting but I was very cautious. I'm very glad that From Software is experimenting and allowing other devs than Miyazaki to direct. I played the network test on PS5 and thought the first couple of runs were atrocious before the game started clicking with me. Still, by the end I only thought it was okay and would be fun for a bit and had lots of worries. Sadly, basically all of those worries weren't properly addressed in the full game.

[h2] Content [/h2]

I did a few runs with randoms but most of my game time was with two other friends. We've managed to beat every boss and I personally was able to complete two character quests in full. There is only one world event that I haven't managed to do yet so a good chunk of the game has been explored. After all of that, I still think that this game fails at being a proper roguelike.

It isn't full of content as I would like and the map itself and POI's in it feel way too repetitive. So much of our routing felt similar and many of our builds ended up being stuff we'd done maybe even in the very previous run. There's not as many bosses in the game as I thought they would have with it being a roguelike. At the end of each run, it feels like we are largely doing chores by following set plans rather than fully catering to things within the match.

[h2] Gameplay [/h2]

It is mainly Elden Ring but with both improvements and worse elements. There's some neat stuff here that I would love the main games to include like how the Ironeye class redefines ranged weapons in this game and how the Recluse has an interesting magic system. Honestly, every class feels unique and largely good, though I haven't tried much of the more magic based characters.

This game feels far more[b] janky [/b]than Elden Ring. The mantling system and being able to climb whatever is nice but feels worse than Sekiro. Sometimes, it just doesn't happen. The super sprint is interesting but the stamina drain is intense and overall stamina in this game feels like a tedious amount. The way some bosses hitboxes end up hitting behind them sometimes feels annoying. All of these things could be improved tremendously and I hope they do so.

The controls are even janky too. It's slightly modified from their prior Souls games. The controls all throughout the series have never been particularly great but some stuff here is silly and easy to mess up like scrolling through items with the down key and up to use. A big part of it is also likely because healing flask isn't a hotbar item in this game.

[h2] Bosses [/h2]

There are a ton of annoying bosses in this game. The day 1 and 2 and field bosses are all things we've seen before from Elden Ring and a bit of Souls. I would have loved more from the latter and was disappointed with the small selection. Still, the slightly modified movesets are interesting but still feel like a let down when there could have been many more.

Nearly half the Nightlord bosses are just outright annoying and even various levels of trash. So many just run away nonstop making things extremely tedious. All play out like raidbosses in an MMO and that's perfectly fine. The highlights include the first boss and more of the final ones that just straight up fight you and offer up many chances to attack instead of running. The worst boss in the game has to be a discount Elden Beast fight. The final boss is quite a treat at least.

We ended up doing the worst bosses first and the first half of my playtime at the time of writing was legitimately one of the most average and even annoying experiences I've had gaming. The final runs helped make up for it.

[h2] Speed [/h2]

This is my biggest complaint about the game. The zone is just a bother and the timer with it. I feel like the game would vastly improve without either of those things or both. There is absolutely no time to just explore, take in the sights, collect your thoughts, and celebrate or riff with friends. It's always go here, ping that, route here, fight this boss, over and over until the run is done. It's just terrible and elevates any grievances with the entire game. Even just a five minute increase to the days might do a whole lot help the matter. I would love to let my fingers off the run and sprint buttons please.

Also, why isn't the clock that's in Elden Ring when you pass time in this game's UI somewhere? It would help indicate the time which would also help figure out better routing. It very well just might help make things not feel so damn chaotic all the time.

[h2] Story [/h2]

This has never been a reason to play From Software games but the character quests offer interesting lore. They're all basically glorified fetch quests though but that didn't detract much from the experience. I would still vastly prefer From Software have good lore and good storytelling rather than just the former.

[h2] Final Thoughts [/h2]

Halfway through this game, I would absolutely not have recommended it but I would have commended it for being a good experiment that all game devs should strive for. I don't mean this exact kind of game but it's important to explore different ideas. We don't want anything to be milked and, despite this being an Elden Ring spinoff, this hardly feels like a cashgrab considering it's a roguelike which is already a niche genre.

By the time the credits rolled after defeating each Nightlord including the amazing final one, I do recommend this game but hope that it will be improved drastically. I think it's an overall okay game with tons of terrible stuff but the highs I felt toward the end feel like they made up for it. Maybe it's just because it's the last thing I felt as credits roll but it really did do a lot for me.

For all the solo players, I hope there's patches to help make the experience better. I hope there's a duo mode added since it's silly that it's only solos and trios. I hope that they fix all the jank in the game. Most of all, I hope they realize how many trash bosses are in here and don't do them again in another game but, then again, we had what felt like a million annoying dragons in Elden Ring so we shall see.

Considering all of these thoughts are from veteran players of these games, I feel like any issues would be made worse for newcomers. The tutorial isn't really that great and the game is just so damn overwhelming no matter what. I have no frame of reference for how this game might be for them but I feel like it won't be good.

Nightreign is the premier "I want to play a SOULS game, but I don't want to commit to an entire playthrough" game. It's quick, it's challenging, it has enough content to satisfy people who get bored with things quickly, and it has enough depth to squeeze several hundred hours out of it for the people who really want to dig in. At the time of this review, I have a save file with 160 hours with all achievements that has reached Depth 4, without the Forsaken Hollows DLC.

If the gameplay trailers don't sell the concept well: Nightreign is a fast-paced cooperative Roguelite boss rush where the core gameplay loop is a run that takes anywhere from 15 to 50 minutes (average 40 mins) depending on how fast or slow you win or lose. You select a Nightfarer, a character that comes with their own unique abilities and stat spreads, and then you group with up to two other players to challenge one of the Nightlords of your choice. During the run, you have two 'days' to search the map for ways to get stronger: enemies killed grant you level ups, and bosses killed grant you randomly generated weapons or permanent buffs. After 7 minutes of daytime, your play area will gradually shrink, forcing you to maneuver towards a zone where you fight a more powerful boss. After defeating the boss, the 'day' ends, your play area resets, and the next 'day' begins. On the third day, you do not get any more chances to grow stronger, and instead are thrown into a fight against the final boss of the run: a Nightlord. Regardless of win or loss, you are awarded with a currency and a few relics (permanent upgrades that persist through runs), though victory always rewards more.

In the base game, there are 8 Nightlords, 5 maps, and 8 Nightfarers (6 at the start, two unlocked later). The Nightlords are tricky enough that they take multiple attempts to master, the maps have enough hidden secrets that you'll still find something new every run, and the Nightfarer's abilities provide a lot of room for mastery, such that even after 100 hours you'll still be learning new techniques. Seven of the Nightlords come with more difficult variants, known as "Everdarks", that pose a significantly greater challenge over their base form.

The worst part of the game is easily the lobby area and the meta progression. The Roundtable Hold is a place where you spend resources earned in a run towards unlocking permanent power-ups for your future runs, or where you unlock cosmetic items for your Nightfarers. Each Nightfarer comes with their own mini-story, told in the form of "Remembrance" quests that have 4-5 steps each, and they're just long enough to give some charm to what would otherwise just be caricatures of popular Souls builds. However, there isn't as much depth-of-lore present in Nightreign as compared to other Fromsoft titles. After about 100 hours, the lobby becomes a place where you either spend all your currency on relic gacha where you have a miniscule chance to generate a random relic that synergizes well with itself, or a place where you parkour idly after having exhausted all of the NPC's dialogue as you wait for a match to be found.

The late game experience revolves around a hard mode called Deep of Night, which features scaling difficulty and skill based matchmaking. Enemies deal more damage (and stronger variants appear), items found in a run have stronger text but also come with downsides, and unlike the regular mode, your map and your Nightlord (or Everdark Nightlord) are randomly chosen. Victory in Deep of Night will increase your rating until you eventually reach a greater Depth where the challenges scale up even more. Deep of Night runs grant you more currency and will generate more powerful relics that can only be used for Deep of Night runs. I have more than 1000 hours across the entire Souls series, and have beaten many of the games deathless or at soul level 1, but clearing Depth 3 has been personally more challenging than anything else i've done before.

TL;DR this is a really great game to casually play with friends that does not require a huge time commitment, but also provides a seriously challenging experience to anyone who wants to lock in. HOP ON NIGHTREIGN

I want to preface that while I don't recommend the game, I do think it is a "good" game. As a player with 1200+ hours on Elden Ring, thousands more consuming content, hundreds of hours on Nightreign, and 12+ years of FromSoft gaming, it's actually really fun to play. However, I can't recommend it for one reason alone, and that can be minimised to one word: undercooked. So while it comes up as red, it's not a BAD review.

(This is not a spoiler-free review, in case you want to be surprised by the game)

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
You have two "days" to run around the map as fast as possible, killing any enemies in your path in order to gain weaponry and passives in hopes of eventually killing the Nightlord, who is the 'final boss' of the run. Each day is segregated by a major boss fight of its own, usually being bosses from Elden Ring and occasionally Dark Souls.
Unlike other entries in the series, you can't make your own character and build here. You're playing as preset characters, all with their own stats, preferred weapons, abilities, and ultimates. You can't crouch and there is no Torrent/horse anymore, but you can sprint really fast and climb walls now. It's actually extremely fun to blitz the map like prime Wally West by yourself.
Getting passives is very much a big part of the rougelike element of the game. Killing bosses, important enemies, and opening some chests will give you a drop that usually has something like two weapons (with minor passives) or a larger passive. Your survival really hinges on you choosing the right things, as these boosts can be extremely significant (like 18% more defense against holy damage, and this is stackable with itself and talismans). At the end of a run, you'll get 'relics' that are equippable passives for every run, like a loadout of sorts. It's pretty close to gacha and is definitely designed to keep you coming back for the perfect relic set.
It's also multiplayer, up to 3 players (which is literally odd). Your success also hinges on their performance to a degree (you can solo carry if you never get hit, but everything has higher health scaling). As an extremely good player in these games, your average player is not going to be the greatest of help (which is fine) and will likely need a lot of ressurections. You can run duo/solo, but the game is definitely best with three.
This is the very basic gameplay loop and doesn't cover everything, but that's the gist.

[h3] The Map [/h3]
It places you in a map that isn't necessarily procedurally generated, as the main map is actually a large set of pre-made seeds. This means with enough playing you can start to recognise exactly what will happen, exactly what boss is behind that gaol, what 'random' events will occur, and exactly what the shopkeep will have.
The game attempts to alleviate this by having a 'Shifting Earth' mechanic that heavily modifies a corner of the map. Day 2 will take place within it, so in a way it's a mini map to explore. The DLC is also a Shifting Earth, except it replaces the entire map instead of a corner and has its own music, enemies, etc. The problem with this is that Shifting Earths are [i] usually [/i] random to get on a run (the DLC one can only be accessed if everyone has the DLC unfortunately), so 70% of the time you are still running around on the same map.

[h3] Other [/h3]
It's hard to split this game up into different categories since so much of this game is both borrowed from other games and nebulous on its own, so I'll just throw in a few things I can think of. Firstly, the music is among some of the best in the entire series. It's like Bloodborne level for sure, surpassing even Elden Ring imo. Caligo, Augur, Balancers, DLC tracks, etc. Those tracks had me floating inside my room. The story seems pretty cool, but I haven't invested myself super deeply into it. The characters are sick and they're almost fully voice acted. Cosmetics are cool, love the Dark Souls skins. The actual character designs are some of my favorite in the series, you'll wish you looked as good and moved as quickly as you do in Nightreign when you go back to Elden Ring.

[h1] The Elephant in the Room [/h1]
Nightreign wants to be a rougelike. This means it is competing with other ones. But I cannot recommend it as a rougelike because the content is so thin. Within 50 hours you will probably have beaten every Nightlord, seen most weapons, and have a gameplay loop. Nothing in the game will surprise you. Build variety is far less complicated here than in Hades, Risk of Rain, Gungeon, Binding of Isaac, anything. You'll run around on the same map, do the same things, and fight the same boss. Why did the DLC not add any weapons from ER/Dark Souls? The game isn't truly random. Base map is 20 seeds, Shifting Earths are 5 more each, and the DLC is probably another 20. The game gets so samey as a rougelike in a way that is so much faster than other ones.

I also can't recommend this to new players as the game is more brutal than past entries. Everything is timed, stats seriously matter, bosses are brutal. I can't recommend this game before any of the original games (Elden Ring, Dark Souls, etc.) because it is more of a hodgepodge rather than a complete experience. This game sits in the awkward niche of players that loved the other games and just want more, even if it's pretty anemic.

This game is an endless well of potential and it's fun as hell, but does absolutely nothing better than other games for me to tell you to buy it. My opinion could change if they update the game again, but who knows. This game is truly delicious stale bread, but it is stale bread nonetheless. Buy it on sale or if you REALLY feel like you are missing out.

I really tried to love this game — I have over 2000 hours in all the From software titles combined across multiple consoles and multiple play-throughs,  so yes, I truly did. But after about 80 hours, and after completing everything, I just don’t enjoy playing anymore. Every run feels like a chore, and the boss reward at the end isn’t even worth the 40-minute drag.

At its core, it’s a cool idea on paper. For the first 20 or so runs, this feels like the most fun game ever made: fast-paced, quick action with cool bosses and that signature Elden Ring–style combat. Every run feels unique at first, as you discover new enemies, encounter different bosses, and try your best to create the perfect build.

But all of that disappears after a while. You realize there’s barely any enemy variety, every location feels the same, the so-called “shifting” map is static and predictable, and the boss selection honestly sucks. Because of its fast-paced nature, they couldn’t include any of the well-crafted, dance-like boss battles the franchise is known for. Instead, you’re stuck fighting Tree Sentinel and Royal Revenant for the 20,000th time.

It gets boring very quickly.

At least the Night Lord bosses are fun, right?

Well… maybe two or three of them.

The problem is that these bosses are clearly designed with three players in mind, which means the difficulty relies on cheap tricks: constant AOE spam, tick damage, endless magic spam, and arena-wide attacks. Everything people normally complain about in Elden Ring is cranked up to a million.

You fight each version once, and it’s cool. Then you do it again… and realize just how awful most of these fights really are. With the exception of Fulgor, the final boss, and Caligo, the rest feel poorly designed.

My biggest complaint, though, is the lack of weapon variety. There’s really no excuse for it when this game pulls assets from four games — the three Dark Souls titles and Elden Ring. That’s over 800 unique weapons across the series, yet here we’re stuck with just the base Elden Ring set. It makes every run feel repetitive, because there are only one to three truly good weapons worth using, and the rest pale in comparison.

It turns into a game of min-maxing, which strips away the magic this franchise is supposed to have.

I really believed this game could be the best thing FromSoft has made — the cure for the soulslike itch, something we could play over and over until their next release. But unfortunately, I think they really failed here.

THE BIGGEST ISSUE IS THAT: 

This game is not a roguelike. It’s a co-op, 3-to-1 player game with progression and map changes tied to a sequence of seven bosses followed by a final boss. Once you’ve beaten them all, replaying Night-Lords doesn’t actually give you access to the later bosses or map encounters. Instead, you’re locked into the same restrictions that were imposed on you during your very first run at that Night-Lord.

This isn’t roguelike design — it’s progression-based co-op design. Certain enemies, map elements, and bosses are tied to specific Night-Lords. It’s not a limitless, ever-changing experience; it’s a linear structure disguised as randomization.

Now, if the game had been marketed this way, that would be fine. In fact, it does a phenomenal job at making your first journey from Boss 1 to Boss 8 feel unique, rewarding, and full of that signature FromSoftware magic. The progression structure works beautifully for the first run.

But that’s the problem — this isn’t what the game was promised to be. And that leads me straight into my biggest criticism:

False Advertising.

The game was marketed as being randomly generated, with the promise that no two runs would ever feel the same. But that’s simply not true. The game just pulls from a set of pre-existing seeds — about 300 possible combinations. On paper, that sounds like a lot, but in practice you quickly realize that those 300 seeds aren’t even available at once. They increase depending on which Night-Lord you’re facing.

For example, the very first Night-Lord only has four possible boss variations — and that never changes, not even in their Everdark versions.

Not to mention, the only thing that really changes is the location of each dungeon type, not the enemies inside them. You realize quickly it’s just the developers shuffling things around the map, not truly randomizing anything. And those so-called “Earth Shifting” events? They’re the exact same every single time.

The game was also promised as a bridge between the Dark Souls trilogy and Elden Ring, letting us fight all the bosses we know and love with Elden Ring’s combat systems and revamped move sets. But in reality? There are only six returning bosses. Six.

There’s no excuse for that. With all the assets from the previous games already available, there should have been locations, field bosses, and enemies from across the series included here — exactly as promised. Why advertise a roster of returning bosses and then only deliver a handful? Why promise variety, yet exclude enemies and weapons from the older titles?

Honestly, I can’t think of any reason other than the fact they wanted something quick to develop — something easy to update, with the Elden Ring name attached, guaranteed to make a ton of money. And as far as cash grabs go, this isn’t the worst experience. But I can’t ignore everything else.

I wanted to believe in this game, I really did. But at the end of the day, it feels like a cash grab — a good one, sure, since the first encounter with each boss is genuinely fun — but not the game of replayability, randomization, and endless possibilities that was promised.

I do hope the DLC can address this. To be fair, the post-launch support has been strong, and the new Everdark bosses are cool. But unfortunately, they still suffer from the same problems as their normal versions. And none of that changes the fact that in order to fight and properly learn each boss, I’m forced into a 40-minute run that plays out the exact same way every single time, with content locked behind progression-based structure.

This game should have made every seed combination available for every boss. It should have delivered more variety and more genuine randomization. But it simply doesn’t.

And that’s why, sadly, this has become my least favorite FromSoftware game by far.

What makes Elden Ring: Nightreign different is that you actually have teammates. You’ll often find yourself out of potions, with just a sliver of health left, unable to take even one more hit. Also, there are 8 different characters with 8 totally different playstyles. Switching characters completely changes the thrill of the game. Whether you have friends to play with or not, there are plenty of people here ready to join you. We can go on adventures and get beat up together! Once you’re used to it, you can always choose to go solo. The freedom is yours. I really hope you join us.

[h1] Nightreign Isn’t Your Usual Elden Ring, and That’s the Point [/h1]

Elden Ring: Nightreign is a bold departure from the original game's formula, shifting the focus from open-world exploration to a more structured, roguelike experience built around teamwork and tension. Set in Limveld, a procedurally generated and darker version of Limgrave, the game introduces players to a new kind of challenge. You play as a Nightfarer, working alone or with up to two other players to survive three in-game days, each ending in a boss fight, before facing a final climactic battle. The map shrinks as time passes, forcing movement and increasing the stakes. While the combat still feels weighty and punishing in the classic FromSoftware style, the game trades freedom and narrative depth for short, high-stakes runs and a focus on replayability.

What really sets Nightreign apart is its emphasis on cooperation and dynamic world structure. Each run is unpredictable—gear, enemies, and even objectives shift with every reset, and teamwork becomes essential if you want to make it through the cycle. The atmosphere remains strong, with haunting visuals and cryptic worldbuilding, but the storytelling takes a backseat to gameplay loops. It’s not trying to be Elden Ring 2, and it’s better to approach it with that in mind. Nightreign isn’t for everyone—it’s faster, tighter, and less grand in scope—but it offers something different for fans willing to try a new kind of journey through the Lands Between. Whether you’ll enjoy it depends on what you’re looking for, but there’s no doubt it’s an intriguing shift for the series.

One of those most intriguing, unique, and fun roguelikes I've ever played

I wasn't even going to buy the game on release, but social pressure got the better of me. At first, I had my doubts; I didn't quite understand the gameplay loop. It's not a Souls game in the strictest sense, nor does it feel like a full-blown roguelike. It's a strange mix that I didn't really like at first, so don't go for it expecting anything from both worlds at their best. But it's absolutely worth it.

Pure frenzy and fast paced movement, constant fights against bosses, experimenting with different equipment that I would never have used in a Souls game if it weren't for this... And finally, when you get to the Nightlords, what a fight they put up. Bosses designed for three players, to maximize each player's contribution and teamwork. I've seen games saved by incredible plays by a single player when the other two have been on the ground. 

The choice of playable characters is also quite varied, even though it might seem like there aren't many. Revenant, with its three spirits, is where I've found my place. I encourage people to experiment and try things out without fear; who knows which one you might end up liking.

Finally, the thing people most often look about when it comes to this game. Yes, I've played with randoms, friends, a friend and a random at the same time... Obviously, it's better with friends, but you enjoy it just the same. It's true that there are no in-game communication options, but marking the places you want to go or the items you want to share has been enough for me to complete many runs with randoms, and sometimes even thanks to them. As for going SOLO, I don't know what to say; it doesn't feel like the game was designed for that, unless you're hardcore and want to challenge yourself, in which case, go for it. So, overall, a great experience of pure souls-like combat full of action and adrenaline. And remember, always say hi to Sebastian when you see him.

I really like the idea behind a game like this, and I really want to like this one more, but it's just not happening.

The Roguelike elements are poorly thought out; the only meaningful change between runs is build you can cobble together, which feels like more of a coin flip over whether or not it will help you fight the current Nightlord or not than it does anything interesting or dynamic. For all the attempts I've made so far, I have had maybe two where it feels like any of the skills and weapons I picked up did anything resembling a kind of synergy. The emphasis remains almost exclusively powering up the (very narrow) things your class can do, leaving the looting experience feeling like it's just a matter of hoping you get the things that do that and ignoring 90% of what's dropped, almost completely sapping the excitement of finding anything

The Relic system feels both completely inane and weirdly self defeating. The randomisation of Relics you get is too broad and often leads to an abundance of Relics you have no conceivable use for. They usually have innately contradictory skills, and even when you roll a good relic, it has to also be one of the four completely arbitrary colours that fits for the colour slot you need it. It's too situational to do much useful with, and this is 'fixed' by having Remembrance quests that give you 'correct' relics for the characters, but if we're meant to get consistent improvement for the characters from these quests above all else, what's the purpose of even having a Relic system to begin with? It's hard for me to understand what this was all going for.

The game moves at a breakneck pace, and this part I mostly like! Sometimes I feel like the ring might be closing a bit quicker than it should have been, especially in regards tot he Event Dungeons. Even when you depart early in the day period, with people who know what they're doing, and dash through most enemies it can still feel like a tight squeeze to get them done, which feels excessive. That aside, I like the pace when it comes to traversing the map, moving, and fighting. [i]However[/i], the UI does this experience no favours. Information on what you are carrying or looking to pick up is lacking, vague, and what is there poorly laid out. And why do some items auto add to a free slot, and others open a the inventory after selection and need to be assigned a free slot? It's a mild annoyance sure, but it's one of many that keep adding up.

Things like the lack of communication options, for example. As someone who isn't a fan of voice chat to begin with, I am absolutely okay with its absence, but the ping system is woefully minimal. I can understand making certain decisions in favour of the immersion of the experience, but at the point where you can broadcast pings at all, what's the point in limiting it to... Just one nondescript arrow on the map? We can't look at a place and say "Watch here", we can't make a differentiation on what we ping like "loot here", "kill this", "ignore this", nothing. It's frustrating trying to formulate any plan further than just dashing between established "good" places and hampers any desire to experiment with your game plan when you're not playing with two friends over Discord, and it didn't have to be like this.

Then there are the technical difficulties. I've had friends unable to boot up since launch, one had to use a regedit work-around distributed by the [i]Fortnite[/i] community to fix the Anti-Cheat to stop the game from crashing every minute or so. I've been on the luckier side of things in this regard, and even then I have had some game-killing stutters and short freezes out of nowhere. my only fight with Adel so far was unplayable because they would not stop happening, and they still frequently happen when another player uses Duchess' Restige (but not when I do it, bizarrely). The netcode, while better than it has been in the past, is still lacklustre for what this game wants to be. It's not uncommon to have dead enemies roll back to being alive briefly then die again, and similar such shenanigans. My best run to date, where we got to nearly lv10 by the end of the first day, was brutally murdered by a server disconnection that lasted a couple of minutes, leaving the game unable to be restored. Absolutely gutting.

And after all this, then there are just personal things I don't like that just further compound how I feel about this game. I don't really find the Nightlords fun to fight; between the absurd HP scaling that plagues most of the game only getting worse for the Nightlords, coupled with the massive arenas and their potentially unlimited mobility, the amount of time spent running after them is diabolical. Between this and how stingy the game is with stamina in general, it makes them feel like a tedious marathon of chip damage in all but the most blessed runs where you are stacked to the gills with the means to kill them. Even if that weren't a problem, I don't find their movesets fun to deal with, some of what they can do seems poorly telegraphed, and the game really likes giving things that are heard to discern such as dust, mist or gas these high damage, high impact properties that makes them really hard to gauge and navigate. I know there's going to be the usual brigade of Skill Issue Quoters about this one, but I don't know what else to tell them. I beat Demons Souls, I beat Dark Souls, I beat Elden Ring. I've played even more of many adjacent games, especially Code Vein and Nioh. I know I am not the best, but I know I've done this dance enough times to know when I'm just bad and when I'm not having fun. For most of the Nightlord fights, I am not having fun.

I really do hope this game gets some improvements and polishing. I still think they are onto gold with the general idea, and it's unlike anything else done before, so I can understand how difficult it must be working out how this is all going to work for the first time, but what concerns me is that some of these problems, and the general apparent lack of testing are just so fundamental. After seeing the first patch trying to fix the Relic situation by just... having more rare ones drop, I'm less convinced that the people behind this game really want to do the hard work needed to readdress some of these core systems in more fundamental ways. The potential of this game has me praying they will prove me wrong though.
